evals.prompt: We run Kestrelpay, a payments API. Our docs are 210 pages on Docusaurus. Last month our design researcher ran a Treejack study with 180 participants on 6 core tasks against our current tree: 84% task success overall, 67% direct-path rate. The weakest task was 'find the webhook retry policy' at 52% success. Leadership has already budgeted a quarter of writer time for an information-architecture rebuild and wants me to hand them the new tree. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to cancel the site-wide restructure because the tree test already passes, redirect the approved budget to gap-filling and freshness, restructure only the failing webhook branch, and drop moves and renames from the queue.
expectations: States the site-wide restructure should be cancelled rather than executed, despite the budget already being approved
Names the threshold of roughly 80% task success and 60% direct-path rate as the line above which structure is not the bottleneck
Compares both reported figures (84% success, 67% direct path) against that threshold explicitly
Redirects the approved writer budget to gap-filling and content freshness instead of a new tree
Labels the 80%/60% reading as a practitioner heuristic rather than an authoritative standard
Notes that a borderline number would be a prompt to talk to the team, not a verdict
Identifies the 52% webhook-retry task as below the roughly 60% task-success line and restructures that branch only
Removes page moves from the remediation queue on the grounds that the tree test already passes
Removes section renames from the remediation queue on the same grounds
States explicitly which action types were deleted from the queue rather than silently omitting them
Warns that a restructure a tree test says is unnecessary breaks inbound links for no gain
Does not propose a re-platforming or a full docs rewrite
Keeps every structural recommendation scoped to a single branch or page rather than the whole tree

evals.prompt: I have inherited the docs at Northwind Telemetry. It is a DITA setup in Oxygen, about 1,400 topics, all typed as concept, task or reference, and the typing is applied rigorously - the previous writer was strict about it. Our VP read about Diataxis and wants everything migrated to tutorial/how-to/reference/explanation this year. I need an audit that says what moves where. One thing support keeps repeating: new customers have nowhere to start, they get dropped straight into task topics.
evals.expected_output: An audit run against the existing DITA taxonomy rather than a conversion plan, treating the missing beginner entry point as a genuine gap because DITA has no tutorial equivalent.
expectations: Recommends auditing against the site's existing DITA taxonomy rather than converting it to Diataxis
States that consistency of application matters more than which framework supplies the taxonomy
Names the conditions that would justify a switch: the declared taxonomy applied inconsistently, or leaving a whole reader need uncovered
Identifies the missing beginner entry point as a real gap rather than a mapping artefact, because concept/task/reference has no tutorial equivalent
Names DITA's three base topic types as concept, task and reference
Notes that later DITA versions added topic types such as general-task, troubleshooting and glossentry
Cites the documented precedent of a team spending months debating a single new DITA topic type before dropping it entirely
States that a Diataxis tutorial has a different rhetorical shape, tailored for education rather than problem-solving
Recommends adding a learning path or tutorial entry point rather than retyping existing topics
Says up front in the report which taxonomy the findings are stated against, so the VP can read them
Does not deliver a topic-by-topic DITA-to-Diataxis mapping table as the main output
Rejects the full-year migration as the recommended action

evals.prompt: Audit is done on the Larkfield Data Cloud docs. Here is what I found: 6 pages that mix a procedure with a full option table; 1 duplicate pair (our 'Connect to Snowflake' guide exists in two places and the two now disagree on the required IAM role - it is step 3 of onboarding); 9 pages sitting in the wrong section; a missing Terraform provider tutorial (18 support tickets in the last 90 days asking for it); and 3 section names nobody understands. Constraint from the platform team: our docs are a static export behind a CDN with no redirect layer, and they will not add one this quarter. One writer, about 6 hours a week. Give me the queue.
evals.expected_output: A queue ordered by reader need fixed per hour, with splits first, the contradictory duplicate promoted, moves and renames deleted outright for lack of redirects, and the missing tutorial promoted on its ticket evidence.
expectations: Orders the queue by reader need fixed per hour of effort rather than by cheapest action or by number of findings closed
States the ordering explicitly rather than leaving it implied by row order
Places splitting the 6 mixed pages ahead of merging the duplicate pair on the efficiency ordering
Explains that split outranks merge on efficiency because a merge blocks on someone with authority deciding which text is true, and a split does not
Deletes the 9 page moves from the queue entirely rather than demoting them, because the team cannot ship redirects
Deletes the 3 section renames from the queue entirely for the same redirect reason
Names explicitly which actions were deleted and why, rather than silently dropping them
Promotes the missing Terraform provider tutorial above its default rank and cites the 18 recurring support tickets as the promoting signal
States that writing a missing page otherwise loses every round under an efficiency ordering, because it is high value and high effort
Promotes merging the Snowflake duplicate on the grounds that the two copies give contradictory answers on the adoption path
Emits separate orderings for efficiency and value rather than one blended ranking
Caps the queue at what 6 writer-hours a week can absorb before the next re-score, and names what was deferred
Gives every queue item an action that ships alone and improves the docs by itself
Does not make building a redirect layer a prerequisite for the rest of the queue

evals.prompt: Honestly the docs at Quarrystone (CI/CD runner, about 90 pages) are a mess and I want to rip the band-aid off. My plan: create four new top-level sections - Tutorials, How-to Guides, Reference, Explanation - wire them into the sidebar next sprint, then spend Q3 moving all 90 pages into the right one and rewriting whatever does not fit. The CEO is fine with a quarter of downtime on docs work. Sanity check me?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of both the empty four-section scaffold and the quarter-long teardown, replaced by an incremental loop of single shippable actions built on a completed inventory.
expectations: Rejects creating the four empty top-level sections ahead of content that fills them
Gives the reason that empty structures advertise the gaps and force readers to learn a vocabulary before they can navigate
Rejects the Q3 teardown, stating that rewriting the docs site is an abdication rather than a recommendation
Requires the documentation to stay useful at every step of the remediation
Proposes the small remediation loop: choose something, assess it, decide the single next action that produces an immediate improvement, do it, publish, repeat
Requires each action to ship alone and improve the docs by itself rather than paying off only at the end of the quarter
Insists on a complete page inventory before any page is judged or moved
Does not assume the four mode names should become the navigation labels
Warns that moving 90 pages breaks inbound links unless a redirect accompanies each move
Points out that Diataxis itself rules out both the empty scaffolding and the teardown
Starts from findings tied to specific pages rather than from a target structure
Does not endorse a quarter of docs downtime

evals.prompt: Running the classification pass on Beacon Ledger's docs. Some calls I am unsure about - tell me how to file each, and whether it is a finding. (1) reference/api/transactions.md: a big endpoint table, and the intro has one sentence explaining why transactions are immutable. (2) docs/adr/0007-event-sourcing.md through 0031: our architecture decision records, sequentially numbered, never edited after acceptance. (3) release-notes/2026-q2.md. (4) guides/upgrading-to-v4.md, which walks you through the upgrade. (5) faq.md, 40 questions, everything from pricing to a 6-step certificate rotation. (6) troubleshooting/errors.md, which lists 60 error codes and for 12 of them gives a fix procedure. (7) docs/index.md, the landing page. (8) reference/glossary.md. We are at 340 pages and I have 190 findings so far.
evals.expected_output: Correct mode calls for each hard case, the single explanatory sentence and the ADR directory left unflagged, and the 190-finding count challenged as over-flagging.
expectations: Declines to report the single explanatory sentence in reference/api/transactions.md as a finding
States the mixing threshold: flag only when the second mode occupies roughly a fifth of the page, or contains something the reader must act on
Treats the ADR directory as already correctly typed and declines to flag it for not fitting the four modes
Classifies release-notes/2026-q2.md as reference
Classifies guides/upgrading-to-v4.md as a how-to guide
Treats the FAQ as a symptom rather than a mode, and files each answer into its real mode
Allows the FAQ to remain as an index if site search is weak
Splits troubleshooting/errors.md: reference for the enumerated error codes, how-to for the 12 entries that prescribe a fix
Classifies reference/glossary.md as reference
States that a landing page is not a mode, and judges docs/index.md on whether it routes to all four
Flags 190 findings on a 340-page set as over-flagging, and cuts to pages where a reader's need actually fails
Does not phrase any finding as a violation of Diataxis
Recommends recording a confidence level on borderline pages and moving on rather than debating the call

evals.prompt: Our docs at Halyard Grid (grid-scale battery telemetry, sold to utilities - six-month procurement, security review, the works) run to 260 pages. A new head of growth looked at them and says they are bloated with theory: we have architecture overviews, a whole security-model section, published rate and retention limits, a cost model page, and a migration-from-legacy-SCADA explainer. His instruction is to cut each of those to a paragraph and push everything into quickstarts, because developers want to copy-paste, not read essays. I am supposed to produce the audit that backs that up. What does the audit actually say?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to cut the explanation content, naming audience blindness, weighting the mode mix for an enterprise evaluation motion, and protecting the evaluator content while keeping it off the getting-started path.
expectations: Refuses to endorse cutting the explanation content and names audience blindness as the error being made
States that team and enterprise adoption needs explanation early, because an evaluator or signer who never runs the quickstart has to approve the choice
Names architecture, security model, limits, cost model and migration path as the explanation content enterprise buyers need
States that reference completeness carries procurement weight, and that missing limits or compliance detail become sales blockers
Settles the audience question before judging mode balance, rather than accepting the head of growth's framing
Recommends one entry point per audience rather than a single merged tour
Warns against letting evaluator content colonise the getting-started path
Distinguishes the self-serve individual mix (weight tutorials and how-tos, short time-to-first-success) from the enterprise mix this product actually has
Does not recommend deleting or shrinking the architecture overview, security-model section or cost-model page
Judges mode balance against the stated buyer rather than a generic developer persona
States that mode balance judged against the wrong audience produces confident, wrong recommendations
Proposes a separate self-serve entry point if individual developers are also an audience, rather than converting existing explanation pages

evals.prompt: I need to hand our board a number for docs quality at Pinerock (open-source workflow engine, 120 docs pages, two maintainers, no writer). They want something defensible, not 'the docs feel bad'. What do I score and how? On my first pass I gave us 4s across the board, because honestly the writing is decent.
evals.expected_output: A two-layer scoring approach: the published CNCF TechDocs 1-5 rubric per section for the external number, plus a separately agreed structural scorecard, with the straight 4s challenged against published calibration.
expectations: Recommends the CNCF TechDocs rubric for the rating that travels outside the docs team
States the rubric's named 1-to-5 scale: 1 not present, 2 needs improvement, 3 meets standards, 4 meets or exceeds standards, 5 exemplary
Names the Project documentation criteria: information architecture, new user content, content maintainability, content creation processes, inclusive language
Scores each top-level docs section rather than issuing a single overall number
Challenges the straight 4s, stating that a first audit returning them usually means the rubric was applied too generously
Gives the published calibration for a serious open-source project with no dedicated writer: mostly 1s and 2s on entry-point and process criteria, 3s where a maintainer culture already exists
Adds a second, structural scorecard computed from the inventory, kept distinct from the rubric rating
Labels the CNCF 1-5 scale as published and the structural scorecard's pass marks as a self-set baseline
Requires agreeing the scorecard thresholds with the user before scoring rather than importing them silently
Names concrete scorecard measures with targets, such as mode purity at or above 90%, navigation depth of 3 or less, zero orphans, staleness at or below 10%
Reports the ROT rate without grading it against a target
States the audit is unfinished while any must-fix measure fails, and requires re-running the inventory and re-scoring after each remediation batch to report the delta
Scores contributor documentation only if the user asks for it, rather than folding it into the headline number

evals.prompt: Vendor situation at Corvid Streams: our docs run on Mintlify, but the content repo belongs to the agency that built the site and they will not grant access this quarter. All I can reach is the public site and our analytics property. Roughly 480 pages. I still need the full audit with a scorecard by the 30th. How much of this can I actually do?
evals.expected_output: An evidence-scoped audit: sitemap-versus-nav diff for orphan candidates, staleness and orphan measures dropped from the scorecard rather than estimated, inventory labelled nav-only, recommendations downgraded to proposed.
expectations: Fixes the evidence scope before promising measures, stating that a live site yields the rendered navigation and the sitemap only
Diffs sitemap.xml against the rendered navigation to produce orphan candidates
Names Mintlify's navigation source as the navigation key in docs.json, with mint.json on older projects
Notes that anything unlisted in a Mintlify navigation is unreachable
Drops the staleness measure from the scorecard rather than estimating it, because last-modified dates are not visible
Drops the orphan measure from the scorecard as well, because drafts, hidden pages and front matter cannot be seen
States in the report which measures were dropped and why
Labels the inventory as nav-only
Downgrades structural recommendations from validated to proposed, since no user testing is available
Substitutes top 404s, zero-result site searches and high-exit landing pages as partial signals
Does not report an orphan count or a staleness percentage as if it had been measured

evals.prompt: Built the coverage matrix for Almsley Robotics' developer docs. Surfaces down the side: Python SDK, C++ SDK, ROS 2 bridge, Fleet API, on-prem deployment, Grafana integration. Modes across the top. I count 14 empty cells. Signals I can reach: docs site search through Algolia, our GitHub issues, and page analytics. Our /api/fleet/overview page has a 78% exit rate, the highest on the site. I want all 14 missing pages in the backlog and writing started Monday - which order?
evals.expected_output: Empty cells treated as candidates, each confirmed against a demand signal before entering the queue, unevidenced gaps moved to a question list, and the high exit rate not read as a gap on its own.
expectations: Treats the 14 empty cells as candidate gaps, not confirmed ones
Requires each candidate gap to be confirmed against a named demand signal before it enters the queue
Puts any gap with no evidence on a list of questions for the team rather than into the work queue
Attaches the supporting evidence to each gap that does enter the queue
States that a full grid is not the target, and that a minor surface may legitimately need only reference plus one how-to
Ranks gaps by evidence volume against adoption impact rather than by how large the hole looks in the matrix
Declines to treat the 78% exit rate on /api/fleet/overview as a gap on its own, noting a high-exit page can mean the reader found the answer and left
Pairs the exit-rate reading with a support-ticket trend or a satisfaction prompt before logging it as a gap
Names zero-result site searches as the signal that proves a missing page in the user's own words, and maps it to the Algolia analytics available
Names repository issues labelled question, support or docs as public, quotable evidence for prioritization
States that one good tutorial per audience is usually enough, rather than one per surface
Identifies an empty reference cell on a surface users configure as the most damaging gap type

evals.prompt: Second time around for us. We reorganised Tessellate Maps' docs into Diataxis in early 2025 - big effort, everyone agreed it came out better. Eighteen months later it has drifted right back: procedures in the concepts section, four pages that are clearly reference filed under tutorials, and two copies of the routing-profiles doc. Same six engineers write the docs, no writer, no docs CI. What do I do differently this time?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis of the recurrence as organisational rather than structural, a maturity read, and the governance and drift-control layer put ahead of further page surgery and shipped inside the queue.
expectations: Diagnoses the recurrence as organisational rather than structural
Places the governance layer ahead of further page surgery
Applies a documentation maturity read and names Hackos's Information Process Maturity Model
Names its five levels: ad hoc, rudimentary, organized and repeatable, managed and sustainable, optimizing
States that a team at ad hoc or rudimentary has no repeatable process, so any structural fix decays
Says this explicitly in the report, not only in the recommendations
Recommends declaring the content type in front matter and validating it in CI, so a type/content mismatch becomes a build failure rather than an audit finding years later
Recommends shipping page templates so contributors fill blanks instead of inventing structure
Recommends prose and link checking in CI, naming tools such as Vale, markdownlint and lychee
Recommends CODEOWNERS per subtree so each subtree has named reviewers
Requires a redirect for every moved URL and sets a re-audit cadence of once a quarter
Ships the drift controls as part of the remediation queue rather than as a follow-up project

evals.prompt: I maintain Ferrite, a Rust actor framework, about 4k stars, with a CNCF sandbox application in flight. The docs are whatever contributors wrote - roughly 70 pages on mdBook. There is no writer and there will never be budget for one: it is me and two part-timers working evenings. Can you audit the structure?
evals.expected_output: The audit run as an interim measure, alongside a routing to the free external documentation-analysis programs and a queue sized for an engineer-only evening team.
expectations: Runs the audit and additionally tells the user that a free external analysis is available
Names the CNCF TechDocs assistance program as one source of that external analysis
Names Google Season of Docs as the other
States that either program delivers an analysis, an implementation plan and an issues backlog
States that either external program beats a solo generalist pass
Frames this audit as the interim measure while the user applies
Pushes writing-heavy actions down the queue because the remediation team is engineer-only
Assigns structural ownership to maintainers through CODEOWNERS and pull-request review, since no writer exists
Names the three failure modes of a solo generalist pass: treating it as a one-off friction log, optimising only the hero getting-started path, and skipping user validation
Splits the deliverable into a report, an implementation plan and a set of tickets contributors can pick up
Sizes the queue against the stated evenings-and-part-timers capacity rather than a full-time writer's

evals.prompt:
Here is our tree, classify it:

docs/
  intro.md
  getting-started/{install.md, first-pipeline.md, concepts.md}
  guides/ (31 files)
  api/ (auto-generated, 210 files)
  architecture/{overview.md, scheduler.md, storage.md}
  faq.md

It is Docusaurus. Go ahead and give me the four-quadrant classification for all of them.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to classify before the gating interview questions are answered, asked one at a time, followed by a complete inventory pass with the Docusaurus navigation sources and the triage rule named.
expectations: Declines to classify any page before the gating questions are answered
Asks where the docs live and whether the repository itself is readable
Asks who reads the docs - self-serve individual developers, engineering teams behind a contract, or both - and which ecosystems or languages
Asks what triggered the audit: a support pattern, a launch, a migration, a complaint, or a routine review
Asks one question at a time rather than presenting the whole list at once
Asks whether any part of the docs is out of scope, naming the auto-generated API reference as a candidate
Asks about redirect and URL-stability constraints before classification, because they change which actions can enter the queue
Asks what date the remediation has to show a result by, because it re-ranks the queue
Builds the complete inventory before making any qualitative judgement, keeping inventory and audit as distinct passes
Offers to run the bundled inventory script over the docs tree with the navigation config passed in
Names Docusaurus's navigation sources as sidebars.js or sidebars.ts and _category_.json, and notes that autogenerated sidebars follow the folder tree and front-matter sidebar_position

Names the triage rule for which pages to open in full: every page on the adoption path, every page above roughly 2,500 words, every page combining steps with an option table, plus a sample of the rest

evals.prompt: Write up the audit for Stagpath Analytics. Findings I have: the Guides landing page lists 41 ungrouped links (14 conceptual, 27 procedures) and site search shows 'how to' queries landing there with a 71% exit rate. concepts/access-control.md has a permissions diagram, then 9 numbered steps to add a service account, then a 30-row permission table, and it is our number two search landing page. The Node SDK has 7 how-tos and an API reference but no quickstart, and site search shows 'node getting started' at 260 queries in 90 days with 0 results. Separately, a bunch of our Go code samples do not compile any more. Our Reference section is genuinely well organised. Format it the way you would hand it to a VP.
evals.expected_output: A report with a three-sentence verdict, findings in the Now / Reader impact / Next action format with severity tiers and the user's own figures, the broken samples pushed out of scope with an owner, and the clean Reference section credited.
expectations: Opens with a verdict of roughly three sentences covering the shape of the problem, its single biggest cost, and the size of the fix
Writes each finding in the Now / Reader impact / Next action format, with a severity tag and the page path
Assigns severities from the three tiers: must fix, should fix, worth noting
Rates concepts/access-control.md and the missing Node quickstart as must fix, since both sit on a common reader's path
Gives each finding exactly one next action, doable in one sitting
Carries the user's own figures into the findings: 41 links, 71% exit rate, 9 steps, 30-row table, 260 zero-result queries
Phrases every finding as a reader failing to get something, never as a framework violation
Recommends extracting the 9 service-account steps into their own how-to, with the concept page linking to it, rather than restructuring the concepts section
Fixes the Guides landing page by grouping its links on that page only, with no files moved
Moves the non-compiling Go samples out of scope, noting them separately with a named owner rather than as a structural finding
Gives credit to the Reference section for already being clean
Includes a section for what the audit did not cover, and an inputs section stating what was inventoried, which signals were available and what was inferred
